title: The Maze
summary: In a maze with walls and empty spaces, a ball rolls until it hits a wall.
statement: In a maze with walls and empty spaces, a ball rolls until it hits a wall. Given the maze dimensions, the ball's starting position, and the destination, determine if the ball can reach the destination by rolling.
constraints: The rectangular maze has 1..100 rows and columns; 0 is open and 1 is a wall. Outside the array acts as a wall.
Start and destination are different open cells given as [row,column]; at least two cells are open.
The ball rolls horizontally or vertically until the next cell is blocked. It may choose a new direction only after stopping.
Return whether it can STOP at the destination. Merely passing through it is not enough.
hints: Search states are stopping positions, not all cells the ball passes.
From each stopped position, roll in all four directions to the next stop.
Use DFS or BFS over those stops, recording visited states and accepting only when a stopped state equals the destination.
An explicit DFS stack avoids recursion-depth limits on large grids. Do not mark intermediate rolling cells as visited stops.
editorial: Each legal roll is one graph edge between stopped positions. Searching that graph explores all possible direction choices while preserving the requirement to stop at the target. The reference uses an explicit DFS stack for deep inputs; recursive DFS teaches the same state definition. The oracle independently simulates one moving cell at a time with a direction in the state, and only permits new directions after a wall creates a stopped state.

tests.explanation: One sequence of complete rolls is left, down, left, down, right, down, right. The final stop is [4,4].
The ball passes [0,2] but stops only at [0,3] or [0,0]. It cannot stop at the requested cell.
